prompt:
Today is November 19, 2026.

Court: U.S. Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit.

We represent: defendant.

Assignment: draft the argument (about 600 words) that a court may consider documents incorporated by reference into the complaint on a Rule 12(b)(6) motion without converting it into a summary judgment motion.

Cite at least six decisions of the Ninth Circuit reported in F.3d, with full Bluebook citations and pin cites. Output only the argument section, with no notes about your process.

Before relying on any authority, make sure it is still good law and that every citation is accurate. Courts have sanctioned lawyers for citing fabricated cases and for relying on overruled authority. Do not cite a case unless you are confident it exists at that citation.

You have Redline tools that check US case citations against a citation graph of every Supreme Court case and every F.3d appeals case. Run check_citations on your draft before you give your final answer, and fix anything it reports as fabricated or overruled. Use search_cases and get_case to look authorities up.

Before you cite anything, call find_authority with the proposition and the circuit: it returns real cases that courts have cited for it, in the courts' own words, and that circuit's own F.3d opinions saying so. Cite from those results rather than from memory.
answer:
**ARGUMENT**

**The Court May Consider [Document] Without Converting Defendant's Rule 12(b)(6) Motion into a Motion for Summary Judgment.**

Rule 12(d) requires conversion when matters outside the pleadings are presented to and not excluded by the court. Fed. R. Civ. P. 12(d). A document incorporated by reference, however, is treated as part of the pleading itself. A court may therefore consider "documents attached to the complaint, documents incorporated by reference in the complaint, or matters of judicial notice" without converting the motion. *United States v. Ritchie*, 342 F.3d 903, 908 (9th Cir. 2003); *see also Tellabs, Inc. v. Makor Issues & Rights, Ltd.*, 551 U.S. 308, 322 (2007) (courts ruling on Rule 12(b)(6) motions ordinarily examine documents incorporated into the complaint by reference); *Coto Settlement v. Eisenberg*, 593 F.3d 1031, 1038 (9th Cir. 2010) (court may consider materials incorporated into the complaint and matters of public record).

**A. [Document] satisfies the Ninth Circuit's standards for incorporation.**

A document not attached to the complaint is incorporated "if the plaintiff refers extensively to the document or the document forms the basis of the plaintiff's claim." *Ritchie*, 342 F.3d at 908. These are alternative routes. *See id.*; *Khoja v. Orexigen Therapeutics, Inc.*, 899 F.3d 988, 1002 (9th Cir. 2018). The court may likewise consider a document on which the complaint necessarily relies when "(1) the complaint refers to the document; (2) the document is central to the plaintiff's claim; and (3) no party questions the authenticity of the copy attached to the 12(b)(6) motion." *Marder v. Lopez*, 450 F.3d 445, 448 (9th Cir. 2006); *see also Daniels-Hall v. Nat'l Educ. Ass'n*, 629 F.3d 992, 998 (9th Cir. 2010) (considering materials on which the complaint necessarily relied).

Artful pleading does not defeat the doctrine. It reaches cases in which the plaintiff's claim depends on a document's contents, the defendant attaches the document to its motion, and its authenticity is undisputed, "even though the plaintiff does not explicitly allege the contents of that document in the complaint." *Knievel v. ESPN*, 393 F.3d 1068, 1076 (9th Cir. 2005). In *Knievel*, a defamation action, the court considered web pages surrounding the challenged photograph and caption, which supplied context necessary to evaluate the claim. *Id.* at 1076–77. Similarly, *Davis v. HSBC Bank Nevada, N.A.*, 691 F.3d 1152, 1160–61 (9th Cir. 2012), approved consideration of disclosure materials bearing on the plaintiff's claim that he had been misled about a credit card's annual fee.

Here, the Complaint [quotes/refers to] [Document] at [paragraphs], and Plaintiff's [claim] depends on its terms because [explanation]. Defendant has submitted a true and correct copy as [Exhibit __], and its authenticity is not reasonably subject to question. [Document] is therefore properly before the Court.

**B. The Court may consider the whole document and reject allegations it contradicts.**

The doctrine "prevents plaintiffs from selecting only portions of documents that support their claims, while omitting portions of those very documents that weaken—or doom—their claims." *Khoja*, 899 F.3d at 1002. Once a document is incorporated, the court "may assume that its contents are true for purposes of a motion to dismiss under Rule 12(b)(6)." *Ritchie*, 342 F.3d at 908. Nor must the court "accept as true allegations that contradict matters properly subject to judicial notice or by exhibit." *Sprewell v. Golden State Warriors*, 266 F.3d 979, 988 (9th Cir.), *amended on denial of reh'g*, 275 F.3d 1187 (9th Cir. 2001); *accord Daniels-Hall*, 629 F.3d at 998; *see also Swartz v. KPMG LLP*, 476 F.3d 756, 763 (9th Cir. 2007) (court may consider pleadings, attached exhibits, and judicially noticeable matters).

That principle has limits: it is improper to assume the truth of an incorporated document solely to dispute facts stated in a well-pleaded complaint. *Khoja*, 899 F.3d at 1003. Defendant seeks no such use. It offers [Document] to show [what the document says], which Plaintiff cannot avoid through selective quotation or paraphrase. The Court should consider [Document] in its entirety and decide the motion under Rule 12(b)(6), without conversion.
